ut.title: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing & UT Inspection | Buffalo, NY
ut.description: Ultrasonic testing in Buffalo, NY: wall thickness surveys, corrosion checks and UT weld inspection on plant, bridge and grain-handling steel. Ask for a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Thickness Inspection in Buffalo, New York
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT performs ultrasonic testing in Buffalo, New York: wall thickness surveys on tanks, piping and process vessels, corrosion checks on structural steel, and shear-wave UT of welds on bridges, crane runways and plant equipment. Buffalo's mix of heavy manufacturing, harbor facilities and bridge crossings produces a steady need for measurements that show what is happening inside the steel. Use the UT quote request to share your asset list and the governing code.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Buffalo

Buffalo grew as a lake port at the end of the Erie Canal, and its waterfront still carries the evidence. The city's grain elevators along the Buffalo River are tall steel and concrete storage structures, and the conveyors, legs, spouts and bins that serve them are steel members that corrode where grain dust and moisture collect. Thickness surveys on corroded steel and checks of repair welds are typical requests from the owners who keep that infrastructure working.

The region's manufacturing base adds a second source of work. Automotive stamping and engine plants on the south side and in Tonawanda operate large presses, boilers, compressed air systems and hydraulic equipment. Smaller steel mills and metal fabricators near Lackawanna and Blasdell use furnaces, ladles, rolls and pressure equipment that wear and crack with time. A heat exchanger shell, a compressed-air receiver or a press frame weld is a normal UT subject.

Bridges complete the picture. Buffalo sits where the Niagara River leaves Lake Erie, and its crossings, from the Peace Bridge to the Grand Island bridges and the Skyway, are steel structures that owners inspect on a regular cycle. The Thruway Authority has planned steel repairs and seismic upgrades on the South Grand Island Bridges, and that kind of work depends on thickness and weld data. Whatever the asset, a good job starts with knowing the nominal wall and the rule that judges the reading.

What UT finds, and what it cannot

An ultrasonic instrument sends a short sound pulse through a probe into the part and measures the time for the echo to return from the far surface or from an internal reflector. In thickness work, that time becomes remaining wall. In weld work, an angled probe aims shear waves through the weld and the technician reads echoes from cracks, lack of fusion and slag. Because the sound travels through the metal, UT sees inside it, which is the main reason it is chosen over surface methods for corrosion and for thick welds.

It has well-known limits. Deep pitting can scatter sound and give an unreliable reading. Scale, loose paint and rust weaken the coupling between probe and steel. Cast iron and heavily alloyed castings attenuate the beam. Cracks that lie parallel to the sound path, or very tight surface cracks, can be missed by an angle-beam scan that is aimed at volumetric flaws, so a part with cracking history is often checked by a surface method as well. See magnetic particle testing in Buffalo and penetrant testing in Buffalo for those companion checks.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Buffalo work

The governing document depends on the asset. Process piping in manufacturing plants usually follows ASME B31.3, with examination in paragraph 344 and acceptance in Table 341.3.2, while power piping falls under ASME B31.1. Pressure vessels are built to ASME Section VIII, and Division 1 Appendix 12 covers UT of welds. Structural steel for crane runways and buildings is welded under AWS D1.1, whose Clause 8 includes UT acceptance for groove welds, and steel bridges fall under AWS D1.5.

The test method is written to ASME Section V. Article 4 covers weld examination, Article 5 covers UT of materials and Article 23 holds SE-797 for contact thickness measurement. ASTM E164 covers contact UT of weldments and ASTM E797 covers thickness measurement. For wall-loss work, our Article 5 explainer outlines the points a procedure should state. If the equipment sits under an API 510, 570 or 653 program, the owner's authorized inspector is responsible and Atlantis delivers the NDE data to that inspector.

State rules matter in Buffalo in an unusual way. The New York State Department of Labor's Boiler Safety Bureau inspects boilers statewide, but its own page notes that the City of Buffalo has a boiler law of its own. Owners of boilers and related pressure equipment in the city should confirm with their insurer or the city which inspection regime applies before scoping NDE. The New York inspection hub summarizes the state picture.

How ultrasonic thickness testing is performed

For corroded steel the technician uses a dual-element probe, which has a transmit crystal and a receive crystal angled toward each other and copes with rough surfaces and pitting. The instrument is calibrated on a step block of matching material that spans the expected thickness range, and the calibration is verified again during the job. An A-scan screen stays visible so that a doubled echo on thin wall or a split in the plate is recognized instead of recorded as a thickness. Readings are taken at the locations the owner defines and recorded against nominal wall and minimum required wall.

Grain-handling and bulk-material steel needs a few adjustments. Surfaces carry dust, coatings and corrosion scale that must be scraped or ground at each test point. Where hot surfaces occur, such as furnace shells or steam lines, a high-temperature probe, suitable couplant and a temperature correction are used. In insulated lines, the owner opens a window in the jacketing before the probe can touch metal.

For weld inspection, a reference level is set from side-drilled holes in a calibration block. The technician selects a 45, 60 or 70 degree shear-wave probe suited to the thickness, scans from one or both sides of the weld, and records the position, length and amplitude of any indication. Where access limits the scan, such as welds on a bridge bearing seat or inside a tight frame, the report states what could not be reached.

Typical Buffalo UT scenarios

A plant on the south side keeps a set of compressed-air receivers and a steam header that its insurer wants measured each cycle. The technician takes thickness readings at the marked locations, compares each against the nominal wall and the previous round, and flags any location where the trend suggests thinning faster than expected. The owner's inspector uses the table to schedule the next visit.

A bridge owner has planned steel repairs on a river crossing. Before cutting out a corroded section of a girder web, the engineer needs a map of remaining thickness around it, so the technician grids the area, cleans each point to bright metal and records readings. After the replacement plate is welded in, shear-wave UT of the new groove welds checks for internal flaws before the paint system goes on.

A grain-handling operator wants to know whether the steel legs of an elevator are safe to keep in service through another season. UT thickness readings on legs and bracing, compared with the original drawings, give the engineer the evidence to decide between repair and replacement. In all three, the scope states which assets, which points and which criteria, so there is no ambiguity about what was and was not measured.

Common reasons a UT result is questioned

Disputes about UT rarely concern the physics. More often a calibration block did not match the material, a probe was worn, couplant was inadequate on a rough surface, or the instrument was left on a setting that suited another job. A reading taken on a laminated plate may reflect the lamination rather than the back wall, and a weld indication read at the wrong beam angle can be mis-sized. The technician's written record of each setting is the defense against these doubts.

Repeatability matters too. If two readings at the same point differ by more than the procedure allows, the technician repeats the measurement and investigates the surface rather than averaging the numbers. A Level III reviews doubtful results before release.

Who performs the work

No Atlantis staff are stationed in Buffalo. Crews travel to your site for the agreed scope and work under the company's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician sets up the instrument and performs and interprets the UT. An ASNT Level III approves the procedures and reviews the reports; that is our founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, who holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT.

Owners who want to build or improve their own program can use written practice development and outside Level III consulting. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

What the UT report contains

The report should let a reviewer repeat the job from the paper. It identifies the component, line or weld, the drawing reference, the procedure and revision, and the code and acceptance table. It lists the instrument, probe type, frequency, couplant and calibration block, and the technician and level. Thickness surveys add a table or grid with nominal wall, minimum wall and each reading, with the lowest readings marked. Weld reports add the beam angle, scan plan, reference level, scanning gain and every recordable indication with location, length and depth.

Each indication or low reading is dispositioned against the named criteria, and any area that could not be scanned is stated. Sketches show where readings and indications sit. The owner's authorized inspector or engineer uses the data to decide remaining life, repair and the next inspection date.

Planning a UT job in Buffalo

Winter is the defining factor. Lake Erie brings cold, wind and lake-effect snow from late fall into spring, and cold steel stiffens couplant and slows instruments. Low-temperature gels, warming the instrument and sheltering the work area keep readings reliable, and snow and ice must be cleared from test points. Outdoor work on bridges or elevators in January is possible, but slower and dependent on safe access.

Summer is warm and humid, and steel in sunlight can be hot enough to need a high-temperature setup. The shoulder seasons of spring and fall give the most workable weather for exterior work and for plant shutdowns, so planning ahead helps. Access often needs scaffold, a lift or rope-access support for bridge steel, silo legs and elevated conveyors, which the owner or its contractor arranges.

Plants require orientation and permits, and bridge work needs traffic control or a track and lane plan set by the owner. Border traffic near the Peace Bridge and the Niagara frontier can slow travel for crews, so allow generous margins. A clear list of asset IDs saves lost time.

UT versus MT and PT for your Buffalo job

Choose UT for wall loss and buried weld flaws. Choose MT for surface cracks in carbon steel welds, such as crane runway welds, press frame repairs and lifting lugs. Choose PT for stainless, aluminum and other nonmagnetic parts. Many jobs combine methods on a single weld. The national UT page, the ultimate UT guide and the MT versus PT comparison help with choosing.

Training your own UT technicians

If you want an in-house UT team, Atlantis offers UT Level 1, UT Level 2 and the broader ultrasonic testing training program. Try the UT simulator for practice. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own technicians, and our courses supply the preparation. See SNT-TC-1A eligibility and NDT training in Buffalo.

faq.q: What can ultrasonic testing do for Buffalo manufacturers and bridge owners?
faq.a: It measures remaining wall on tanks, piping, vessels and structural steel, and it examines welds for internal flaws such as lack of fusion. Results go into the owner’s repair, replacement and inspection planning.

faq.q: Can you gauge corroded steel in grain-handling equipment?
faq.a: Yes. Spouts, legs, bins and conveyor frames can be gauged with a dual-element probe after the test points are cleaned of dust and scale. Readings are recorded against nominal wall by location.

faq.q: Which standards apply to UT of welds on bridge steel?
faq.a: Steel highway bridges are welded under AWS D1.5, and the owner’s specification sets the acceptance classes. The UT procedure is written to ASME Section V Article 4 unless the contract names a different method document.

faq.q: Does Buffalo have its own boiler inspection rules?
faq.a: The New York State Boiler Safety Bureau’s website says the City of Buffalo has its own boiler law. Confirm the regime with your insurer or the city, and we will scope the NDE accordingly.

faq.q: Is there an Atlantis office in Buffalo?
faq.a: No. Crews are mobilized from outside the city once the scope is agreed. Please include the address, access rules and any border or badging needs in your enquiry, and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Can UT be carried out in winter at Buffalo sites?
faq.a: Yes, with low-temperature couplant, a warmed instrument and clear test points. Heavy snow, wind or ice may stop exterior work for safety reasons, and the schedule should leave room for weather.

faq.q: Who is the inspector of record on API equipment?
faq.a: The owner’s authorized inspector. Atlantis performs the UT and passes thickness and indication data to that inspector, who judges fitness for continued service and sets the next inspection date.

faq.q: What should I send to get a UT quote for a Buffalo site?
faq.a: Send the asset list, nominal wall, material, operating temperature, governing code, access details and target dates. Prior thickness readings help us compare against a baseline and plan test points efficiently.

faq.q: Can you train technicians at our Buffalo plant in UT?
faq.a: Atlantis offers UT Level 1 and Level 2 training. The employer certifies its own personnel under SNT-TC-1A, so the course is preparation that feeds the employer’s program and not a certificate in itself.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Buffalo, NY | MT
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection in Buffalo, NY: mag particle testing of welds, press frames, crane steel and bridge repairs. Describe your parts for a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Buffalo, New York
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT provides magnetic particle inspection in Buffalo, New York. Mag particle testing finds surface and near-surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel, so it suits the press frames, crane runway welds, structural repairs and equipment attachments that Buffalo's industry depends on. Share part details through the MT quote request and we will return a scope for your review.

Where magnetic particle testing is used in Buffalo

Buffalo's industrial heritage still shows in its steel. Automotive stamping and engine plants run large presses and crane-served bays, and the welds on press frames, crane girders and runway rails are cyclically loaded, which is what produces fatigue cracks. MT is a quick way to look at a weld toe or a repair after grinding and tells the maintenance team whether a crack is present.

The waterfront and the grain trade add structures of their own. Steel legs, spouts and bin supports in grain-handling facilities along the Buffalo River experience vibration and corrosion, and repairs to attachments and brackets are often followed by MT. Port equipment, rail cars and rail track work in the city's yards add lifting lugs, couplers and structural welds.

Bridges are the third big category. Steel repairs on the Grand Island bridges and other river crossings include weld repairs on members that carry heavy traffic loads, and MT of repair welds is a standard check before the member returns to full service. Fabrication shops serving this work also use MT on shop welds before blasting and painting.

What MT finds, and what it misses

MT works by magnetizing the part and exposing leakage at a discontinuity. When a crack crosses the magnetic field, the field spills out of the steel at the break, and iron particles dusted or sprayed on the surface gather there and outline the flaw. The technician sees an indication within seconds of applying the particles, which makes the method quick and easy to repeat.

The same physics sets its limits. Only ferromagnetic metals respond, so carbon and low-alloy steel are suitable while austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and copper alloys are not. For those materials, see penetrant testing in Buffalo. MT finds flaws at or just below the surface but cannot measure depth or detect deep buried flaws, which is when ultrasonic testing in Buffalo is used. Paint, scale and weld spatter lower sensitivity, so the technician checks the surface and the owner removes what is needed.

Codes and acceptance criteria

ASME Section V Article 7 sets the method requirements, and the construction code supplies the acceptance limits. For pressure vessels under ASME Section VIII Division 1, Appendix 6 gives MT methods and acceptance. Process piping under ASME B31.3 uses paragraph 344.3 and Table 341.3.2, and power piping follows B31.1. Structural steel is governed by AWS D1.1 and bridge steel by AWS D1.5, each with its own surface-examination provisions. ASTM E709 is the guide for MT and ASTM E1444 the standard practice.

For a short summary of the method's rules, see our guide to Article 7 magnetic particle requirements, and for background the complete MT guide.

New York State's Department of Labor administers boiler regulations statewide, but its website states that the City of Buffalo has its own boiler law, so owners with boilers or pressure equipment in the city should confirm the applicable regime. See the New York inspection services hub. Where API 510, 570 or 653 programs apply, the owner's authorized inspector is accountable and Atlantis performs the MT and passes on the findings.

How magnetic particle inspection is done

In the field the technician uses an electromagnetic yoke, a portable device with two articulated legs that induces flux in the part between them. The yoke is lift-tested before use to prove that it has enough strength at the pole spacing in use, and the weld is examined twice with the legs turned about ninety degrees so cracks in any direction are caught. For heavy sections or special geometries, prods or a coil may be specified.

Particles can be dry powder in contrasting colors, which suits rough outdoor surfaces, or wet particles in a liquid carrier, which gives finer sensitivity on smoother surfaces. Fluorescent wet particles show cracks as glowing lines under UV-A light in a darkened area. Where contrast is poor, a thin white paint on the surface behind black particles makes indications easier to see. The procedure specifies the field strength, dwell and viewing conditions.

After testing, parts that will be welded again, machined or placed near sensitive equipment may need demagnetizing. A field meter verifies the residual level. Particles are cleaned from the surface before painting so coatings adhere.

Who performs the work

Atlantis keeps no staffed site in Buffalo, so a Level II technician is mobilized to your premises for each job, working under the company's written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. The technician sets up the equipment, performs the examination and interprets the indications. An ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports, and our founder Anoop Rayavarapu holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT.

If your own written practice needs attention, see written practice development and Level III consulting. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

What the MT report contains

The report names the component or weld number, the drawing, the procedure and revision, and the code and acceptance table. It records the technique (yoke, prods, wet or dry, visible or fluorescent), the particle product and batch, the equipment with its lift-test or calibration status, field direction, surface condition, the technician and level. Each indication is described by location, length and orientation, shown on a sketch or photo, and dispositioned against the acceptance criteria.

The report notes whether the part was demagnetized, and a Level III reviews and signs it. The owner's engineer or inspector decides on repair, further testing or release.

Typical Buffalo MT scenarios

A stamping plant maintenance team finds a hairline crack indication on a crane girder at the toe of a stiffener weld. The weld is ground, MT confirms whether any crack remains, and the process repeats after the repair weld cools. The report supports the decision on whether the crane returns to service.

A bridge repair contractor welds replacement steel into a truss member. The repair welds are examined by MT after dressing and before painting, with the acceptance table from the owner's specification applied. The owner's engineer reviews the report and decides on release.

A grain facility replaces a bracket on a bucket elevator leg. The new fillet welds and the original welds near them are inspected by yoke, with the technician noting any pre-existing cracks in adjacent steel so they are repaired at the same visit. The scope for each job names the welds, the sampling percentage and the criteria.

Planning an MT job in Buffalo

Cold is the main variable. Wet baths and contrast paint are made for a working range, and below it particles move sluggishly and paint can lift off. Buffalo winters demand warming the part, a product suited to cold, or a pause. Sheltered setup helps with wind and snow that otherwise blow dry particles off the part. In summer, hot steel dries the carrier too fast and weakens fluorescence.

Fluorescent MT needs darkness, so outdoor work usually calls for a tent or shroud, or a scheduled dark window. Plants require orientation, permits and badge checks. Bridge work needs access equipment and traffic control arranged by the owner, and the border crossing near the Peace Bridge can slow crews who travel into the area.

Provide a clean test surface, power if a bench unit is needed and a clear weld map, and plan around shutdown windows in spring and fall.

Common reasons a magnetic particle result is questioned

Disputes about MT usually trace back to technique. A yoke used at a wider spread than the lift test covered, a weld examined in a single direction, particles applied to a wet surface, a fluorescent examination under too much ambient light, and an indication judged without the lighting the procedure required all give a result that a reviewer can reasonably challenge. Sharp changes in section, magnetic writing and edges can create non-relevant indications that look like cracks until they are resolved by re-testing.

The record is the protection. The report states field direction, yoke verification, light levels, particle batch and surface preparation, so the reviewer sees the examination was done as written. Borderline indications go to the Level III instead of being decided alone, and the technician re-magnetizes after demagnetizing when an indication must be proved real.

MT versus PT and UT in Buffalo

MT is the fastest check for surface cracks in magnetic steel. PT is the choice for stainless, aluminum or rough parts that cannot take particles. UT is the choice for wall loss and flaws below the surface. See the MT versus PT comparison and the national MT page for more.

Training your own MT technicians

Atlantis teaches MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 within the magnetic particle testing training program for employers building their own teams. The employer certifies under SNT-TC-1A. See NDT training in Buffalo and practice tests for exam preparation.

faq.q: What does magnetic particle inspection cover in Buffalo?
faq.a: Surface and near-surface cracks in welds, lugs, press frames, crane steel and bridge repairs in carbon or low-alloy steel. The part must be ferromagnetic and the surface clean enough for particles to move freely.

faq.q: Can MT be used on stainless steel or aluminum parts?
faq.a: No, those alloys are not magnetic. Liquid penetrant testing covers surface-breaking cracks in them, and ultrasonic testing is the choice for internal flaws and wall loss.

faq.q: Which standard sets the method for MT of welds?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 7 sets the method. Acceptance limits come from the construction code, such as ASME Section VIII Appendix 6 for vessels, B31.3 for piping, or AWS D1.1 and D1.5 for structural and bridge steel.

faq.q: Can you do fluorescent MT outdoors in Buffalo?
faq.a: Yes, with a tent or shroud that gives the darkness the procedure requires, or by scheduling at night. Visible particles are the alternative where darkness cannot be arranged.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Buffalo?
faq.a: No. We send a technician to your address when the scope is agreed. Send the access rules and any border or badge needs with your quote request and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Do you demagnetize parts after MT?
faq.a: When the procedure or owner requires it, for example before welding, machining or coating. A field meter confirms the residual level and the report records the result.

faq.q: How does Buffalo winter affect MT?
faq.a: Cold slows particles and can thicken carriers. We warm the part, change product or use dry particles, protect the area from wind and snow, and record surface temperature so the result is defensible.

faq.q: What should I send to get an MT quote for a Buffalo site?
faq.a: Send the weld or part list, material, coating, governing code and acceptance table, access details and target dates. A photograph of a typical weld helps us choose technique and equipment.

faq.q: Do you train people in MT?
faq.a: Yes. We run MT Level 1 and Level 2 training for employers. The employer certifies its own people under SNT-TC-1A, and our course supplies the theory and hands-on preparation.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection & Liquid Penetrant | Buffalo, NY
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing in Buffalo, NY: dye penetrant inspection of stainless, aluminum and steel welds, castings and machined parts. Request a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) and Dye Penetrant Inspection in Buffalo, New York
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT provides liquid penetrant testing in Buffalo, New York. Dye penetrant inspection shows cracks and pores that are open to the surface on welds, castings, forgings and machined parts, whether the metal is carbon steel, stainless, aluminum or nickel alloy. A technician is mobilized to your site, follows a written procedure and reports each finding against the code. Start with the PT quote request.

Where penetrant testing is used in Buffalo

Buffalo's metalworking tradition means a lot of machined and cast parts. Foundries, machine shops and metal fabricators around the city and in Tonawanda and Lackawanna turn out castings, forged flanges, shafts and housings that benefit from a final surface check. Penetrant testing is the standard method for aluminum and nonferrous castings and for parts that cannot be magnetized.

Food and beverage processing, a large employer in the Buffalo area, uses stainless steel tanks, piping and equipment, where weld cracks are both a structural risk and a sanitary risk. Cereal and flour milling operations use stainless and carbon steel equipment too. PT of stainless welds after fabrication or repair gives a reliable surface check without introducing a risk to the process.

Power and manufacturing plants add pump and valve bodies, boiler tube attachments, and nonmagnetic alloy parts, while the transportation sector adds aluminum components and stainless hardware. Wherever the material is not suited to magnetic particles, PT is the usual surface method.

What penetrant testing finds and what it misses

The method relies on capillary action. A thin liquid is applied to a clean dry surface and enters any opening. After a set dwell time, the excess is removed and a developer is applied; the developer draws trapped liquid out so a crack appears as a colored or glowing line against a contrasting background. Fine tight cracks, which the eye cannot see, can be revealed this way on a wide range of metals.

The limits follow from the principle. A flaw must reach the surface or PT sees nothing, so buried lack of fusion, wall thinning and internal cracks are outside its scope. Machining, grinding and shot peening can smear metal across a crack opening and hide it, and heavy paint, scale or oil blocks entry. Porous surfaces absorb penetrant and can create a confusing background. Ferromagnetic parts are often checked faster with MT in Buffalo, and internal flaws or wall loss need UT in Buffalo.

Codes and acceptance criteria

ASME Section V Article 6 covers the liquid penetrant method. For pressure vessels built to ASME Section VIII Division 1, Appendix 8 gives PT methods and acceptance. For piping, ASME B31.3 calls for PT under paragraph 344.4 and sets its limits in Table 341.3.2. ASTM E165 is the standard practice for general industry, while AWS D1.1 and D1.5 set the weld quality for structural and bridge steel. Our guide to Article 6 penetrant requirements explains the rules, and the national penetrant page covers the method.

Work on stainless steel and nickel alloys often calls for penetrant materials with low sulfur and halogen content, so residues do not damage the metal during later heating. The procedure names the product family and contaminant limits, and the report records batch numbers.

Under New York State's boiler program, the Department of Labor Boiler Safety Bureau certifies welded-repair facilities and inspects boilers, while its website notes that the City of Buffalo has its own boiler law. Owners should confirm the regime for their equipment. See the New York inspection services page. Under API 510, 570 and 653 programs, the owner's authorized inspector stays responsible and receives our PT data.

How dye penetrant inspection is performed

Cleaning comes first. The technician removes paint, oil, scale and spatter by grinding, wire brushing or solvent, then dries the surface. Visible dye penetrants (Type II) are red and viewed in white light; fluorescent penetrants (Type I) are viewed under UV-A in a darkened area for higher sensitivity. Solvent-removable penetrant is the usual field choice since it needs no water, while water-washable and post-emulsifiable systems suit shop work and large batches.

Dwell time follows the procedure, typically in the range of several minutes to half an hour depending on material and expected flaws. The excess is wiped with care so that penetrant is not drawn out of a crack, and a thin even coat of developer is applied. After the developing time, the technician examines the surface in good light and records indications by type, location and size.

Part and product temperature matter. The standard procedure covers a working window of cool-to-warm shop conditions; outside it, the process must be shown to work with a comparator block that has known cracks. The technician runs that check at the start of work and when conditions change.

Who performs the work

Nobody from Atlantis is stationed in Buffalo. Technicians travel to your site once the scope is agreed and work under the company's written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician performs and interprets the examination. An ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Our founder is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

For owners who want a program of their own, see written practice development and Level III consulting.

What the PT report contains

The report names the component or weld, the drawing, the procedure and revision, and the code and acceptance criteria. It records the penetrant type and method and the manufacturer and batch of penetrant, cleaner and developer. Surface and ambient temperature, dwell and developing times, UV intensity or white-light level, and the comparator check are all entered. Each indication is described by shape, location and size, shown on a sketch and dispositioned as acceptable or rejectable.

The technician, qualification level and date are included, and a Level III review is noted where the contract requires it. The owner or its engineer decides on repair and re-examination.

Typical Buffalo PT scenarios

A food plant has repaired a weld on a stainless process tank. After grinding the repair flush, the weld and its heat-affected zone are cleaned and examined by PT, then cleaned again so no residue remains in the product zone. The report records the cleaning steps and products, so the plant's quality team can file it.

An aluminum casting shop wants to check a lot of housings before shipping. A sample or the whole lot is examined by fluorescent PT after machining, and indications are marked and measured against the customer's acceptance standard. A comparator block verifies the process on the day.

A power plant has replaced a nozzle in a stainless steam line. The nozzle weld is examined by PT using low-halogen materials, and the batch numbers are written on the record so material control can be shown if later questioned. In each case the scope states the parts, the standard and the cleaning requirements.

Planning a PT job in Buffalo

Temperature drives the plan. In winter, steel in an unheated shop or open yard can be far colder than the standard working window, and penetrant becomes thick while developer clings poorly. The choices are warming the part, using a qualified low-temperature system, or waiting; doing nothing is not an option. In summer, sun-heated steel dries solvent faster than it can enter a crack, so shade or cooling is used.

Lake-effect snow and wind interfere with developer application, and humidity can dull the contrast. Fluorescent PT needs a dark enclosure. Plants require badge checks and permits, and confined-space work needs ventilation for solvent vapors and gas monitoring. Border-area traffic can add travel time for crews.

Give us the weld or part list, state the sequence if PT must follow grinding or precede coating, and plan around shutdowns in spring and fall.

Common reasons a penetrant result is questioned

Questions about PT usually point to process. Penetrant that dried in the sun, over-cleaning that washed a crack empty, a heavy developer coat that masked a fine line, or oil left in a crack that blocked entry each produce a result that can be challenged. False indications from a rough weld toe, a scratch or a bleed-out from a porous area can resemble cracks, so the technician wipes and re-develops to see whether the line returns.

The written record answers those doubts: times, temperatures, product batches and the comparator result are all entered. If a result is unclear, the technician repeats the whole cycle from cleaning, and a Level III reviews anything marginal. Surface history matters too, so tell us if the part was blasted, peened or machined before arrival, because smeared metal may need a light etch to reopen cracks.

PT versus MT and UT in Buffalo

PT is the right choice when metal is nonmagnetic or when the most sensitive surface check is needed on a clean weld. MT is faster on carbon steel and can find slightly subsurface flaws. UT handles wall loss and internal flaws. The MT versus PT comparison sets out the trade-offs.

Training your own PT technicians

We teach PT Level 1 and PT Level 2 within the penetrant testing training program, with a PT simulator for practice. The employer certifies its own people under SNT-TC-1A. See NDT training in Buffalo and practice tests.

faq.q: What does liquid penetrant testing find in Buffalo plants and shops?
faq.a: Surface-breaking cracks, laps, pores and seams on welds, castings, forgings and machined parts in steel, stainless, aluminum and other nonporous metals. Flaws that do not reach the surface cannot be seen.

faq.q: When should a Buffalo owner choose PT rather than MT?
faq.a: Choose PT for stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys or any part that is not magnetic, and for rough surfaces unsuited to particles. MT is usually faster on carbon steel and can detect slightly subsurface cracks.

faq.q: Which standards cover liquid penetrant inspection?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 for the method, ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for vessel acceptance, B31.3 paragraph 344.4 for piping, and ASTM E165 as the general practice. AWS D1.1 and D1.5 cover structural and bridge welds.

faq.q: Can PT be done in Buffalo in winter?
faq.a: Only when the process is shown to work at the temperature. We warm the part, use a qualified product or reschedule, and record the surface temperature so the result stands up to review.

faq.q: Is there an Atlantis office or lab in Buffalo?
faq.a: No. Technicians travel in when the scope is agreed. Include the address, access rules and any border considerations in your enquiry and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Do you control sulfur and halogens on stainless work?
faq.a: Yes, when the specification calls for it we use low-contaminant materials and record the manufacturer and batch so you can show they were controlled. Tell us the alloy in your request.

faq.q: How should surfaces be prepared before PT?
faq.a: Remove paint, oil, scale and spatter and dry the surface. If grinding or blasting was done, tell us, because smeared metal can close cracks and may need etching or removal before testing.

faq.q: What do I send for a PT quote for a Buffalo site?
faq.a: Send the part or weld list, material, size, surface condition, code and acceptance criteria, location and access details. Photos of a typical weld help us pick the penetrant system and lighting.

faq.q: Can you train our technicians in PT?
faq.a: Yes. We offer PT Level 1 and Level 2 training for employers qualifying people under SNT-TC-1A. The employer certifies its own personnel, and our course provides the theory and practice.
